name: Metamorphic rock
ph: Soil pH 4.5–6.0, depending on the member
tagline: Older rock changed in place by heat and pressure, deep in the crust, without ever melting.
forms: Burial, mountain building or the heat of a nearby intrusion pushes rock past the point where its minerals are stable. They break down and regrow as forms that are stable at the new conditions, usually lining up with whatever direction the pressure came from.
type: Metamorphic rock — one of the three great rock families
madeOf: Depends on the parent: calcite in marble, quartz in quartzite; mica, quartz, feldspar, garnet and amphibole in schist and gneiss.
grain: From microscopic (slate) to coarse (gneiss, marble). Many are foliated, with minerals lined up in sheets or bands; others, like marble and quartzite, are interlocking crystals with no direction.
colour: Inherited from the parent rock: white marble and quartzite, grey slate, glittering schist, banded gneiss.
luster: Often shinier than the parent rock: mica gives schist and phyllite their sheen, and recrystallised calcite and quartz glitter.
streak: Varies with the rock, from white (marble) to grey (slate); quartz-rich rocks just scratch the plate.
hardness: From about 3 (marble) to 7 (quartzite); foliated rocks are often soft along their mica layers.
density: Varies too much for one figure — mostly about 2.6 to 3.0 g/cm³, and metamorphism generally leaves a rock denser and more compact than it was.
porosity: Generally very low — metamorphism squeezes out pore space — so water moves mainly through cracks.
acid: In places — only where calcite is part of the mix.
formsFrom: Any older rock — igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic — changed by heat, pressure or hot fluids without melting.
becomes: Migmatite if it partly melts, and magma if it melts entirely; sediment once it is worn down at the surface.
world: In the cores of mountain belts and the ancient shields of every continent.
what: The family of rocks whose minerals regrew in the solid state. Some maps say only this much, which still tells you the rock will be hard, probably striped or sheeted, and will not hold fossils.
identify: Minerals aligned into sheets, stripes or a visible grain, with no bedding and no fossils. Generally harder than the rock it came from.
wears: Slowly, and along whatever grain the squeezing gave it.
above: Generally thin, stony soil on hard ground, usually acid, with lakes wherever a hollow holds water.
where: The Canadian Shield, the Appalachians, and the cores of every western range.
lives: Conifer and hardwood forest on thin soil, and acid-water lakes — unless a limey band runs through, in which case everything changes for its width.
uses: Building stone, roofing, aggregate and abrasives.

faqs.a: Rock that has been changed by heat, pressure or hot mineral-rich fluids — usually deep underground or where plates collide — without melting. Its minerals regrow in new forms, making a denser, more compact rock.

Two main ways. In regional metamorphism, rock is buried deep in a colliding mountain belt and squeezed and heated. In contact metamorphism, hot magma bakes the rock beside it, with little pressure, making rocks such as hornfels.

faqs.q: What is the difference between foliated and non-foliated metamorphic rock?
faqs.a: Foliated rocks have minerals lined up in sheets or bands because pressure squeezed them — slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss. Non-foliated rocks have no such direction, usually because their minerals do not grow as flat crystals — marble and quartzite.

faqs.q: What are examples of metamorphic rocks and what they come from?
faqs.a: Shale becomes slate, then phyllite, schist and gneiss as the heat rises. Sandstone becomes quartzite. Limestone and dolostone become marble. Basalt becomes chlorite schist or amphibolite. Granite becomes gneiss.

name: River deposits
ph: Soil pH 6.0–7.5, inherited from whatever is upstream
tagline: Sand, silt and gravel dropped by a river and still being dropped — the youngest ground there is, and the most fertile.
forms: A river carries what its current can lift and drops it the moment the current slackens — on the inside of a bend, across a floodplain in flood, or where it meets a lake or the sea. Every flood adds a layer.
type: Surficial deposit — alluvium (loose river sediment)
madeOf: Whatever the river has eroded upstream — commonly quartz and feldspar sand, pebbles of local rock, and clay.
grain: Sorted by the current: gravel and sand in channels and bars, finer sand and silt spread over the floodplain, clay in the backwaters. Grains are rounded by the journey and laid in visible layers.
colour: Browns, greys and tans, taking the colour of whatever rock lies upstream; darker where plant matter has built up on the floodplain.
luster: Not a rock, so no luster of its own; quartz sand grains glint.
streak: Not a streak material — its mud smears in the colour of its clay, usually grey to brown.
hardness: Not rock: each pebble has its own hardness, but the deposit itself digs with a spade.
density: Varies with grain size, packing and water; there is no single figure for loose sediment.
porosity: High: sand is typically 20–35% open space, gravel 30–40%, silt 35–50% and clay 33–60% — but water flows easily only through the sand and gravel.
acid: In places — only where calcite is part of the mix.
formsFrom: Rock and soil weathered and eroded upstream, carried by the river and dropped where the current slows.
becomes: Conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone and shale if it is ever buried and cemented; until then, the river keeps picking it up and setting it down.
howLong: Being laid down now: every flood can add a layer, and most alluvium is geologically very young.
world: Along every river and in every delta and floodplain on Earth.
what: Alluvium: loose sediment laid down by moving water on a floodplain, a delta or a bar. Some of it is decades old rather than millions of years.
identify: Loose, sorted by size into visible layers, rounded grains, and flat ground beside a river. Dig a hole and it does not stop.
wears: It is already weathered; that is what it is. The river sorts it, moves it, and puts it down somewhere else.
above: The deepest, most fertile and most level soil in any landscape, which is why floodplains are farmed and towns get built on them. Also the ground that floods, and the ground that liquefies in an earthquake.
where: Every river valley, the Mississippi and Fraser deltas, the Central Valley of California, and the flats every prairie town sits on.
lives: Silver maple, cottonwood, willow and ostrich fern; the richest foraging ground in most regions, and the first to be ploughed.
uses: Farmland, and the sand and gravel that every road and building is made of.

faqs.q: What are deposits of sand, gravel and soil left by rivers called?
faqs.a: Alluvium, or alluvial deposits: clay, silt, sand and gravel laid down by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in deltas and in fans at the foot of mountains. It is geologically young, and on active floodplains it is still being laid down.

faqs.q: Where do rivers drop sand and gravel?
faqs.a: Wherever the current slows: on the inside of bends, on bars in the channel, across the floodplain when the river overtops its banks, and where it enters a lake or the sea to build a delta. Heavy gravel settles first; fine silt and clay last.
Yes. Sand and gravel are typically 20–40% open space and let water flow freely, so wells in them often yield well. Floodplain silt and clay hold even more water by volume, but give it up slowly.

name: Glacial till
ph: Soil pH 5.5–7.5, inherited from wherever the ice came from
tagline: Everything a glacier carried, dumped where it melted — clay, sand, gravel and boulders, mixed with no sorting at all.
forms: An ice sheet grinds up whatever it crosses and carries the debris frozen into its base. When it melts, all of it drops at once, in place. Where the ice was also pressing down, the result is compacted into a dense layer that has barely loosened since.
type: Surficial deposit — sediment dropped directly by glacial ice
madeOf: Anything the ice crossed: ground-up local bedrock mixed with stones and boulders (erratics) carried from outcrops as much as hundreds of kilometres away.
grain: Unsorted: clay, silt, sand, gravel and boulders all mixed together with no layering, often with a high share of silt and clay. Stones range from angular to partly rounded.
colour: Grey, brown or buff, taking its colour from the rock the ice ground up.
luster: Not a rock, so no luster of its own.
streak: Not a streak material; its clay smears grey to brown.
hardness: Not rock. Lodgement till, packed down under moving ice, is very dense and can be hard to dig; ablation till is looser.
density: Varies; lodgement till is very dense for a loose deposit, while ablation till is looser.
porosity: About 10–20% open space, but the fine clay and silt clog the pores, so till is only slightly permeable — a domestic well in till may yield only about 4–38 L (1–10 US gallons) a minute.
acid: In places — only where calcite is part of the mix.
formsFrom: Bedrock and older sediment scraped up, ground and carried by an ice sheet or glacier, then dropped as the ice moved or melted.
becomes: Soil at the surface; if it is ever buried and hardened, a sedimentary rock called tillite.
howLong: Most surface till in Canada and the northern US was left by the last ice sheet, which reached its farthest south about 23,000 years ago — building the moraines of Long Island and Cape Cod — before melting back.
world: Wherever ice sheets or glaciers have been, and below every glacier melting today.
what: Sediment released directly from ice rather than from water. Because ice carries everything at the same speed, nothing gets sorted: a boulder sits in clay beside a pebble.
identify: Unsorted — that is the whole test. Mixed grain sizes with no layering, angular and rounded fragments together, and boulders of rock that does not outcrop anywhere nearby.
wears: Compacts rather than drains. The fine fraction packs into a hardpan that both roots and water struggle through.
above: Stony, uneven, often poorly drained ground, with boulders that keep surfacing in ploughed fields. Its chemistry comes from wherever the ice was scraping, so it can be sweet ground sitting on sour bedrock, or the reverse.
where: Everywhere north of the last ice limit — nearly all of Canada (parts of the Yukon were never glaciated), New England, the Great Lakes states, and the northern plains.
lives: Mixed forest and pasture; the wet hollows in it hold the sedge meadows and alder swamps that much of the north's wildlife depends on.
uses: It is what most of northern North America farms and builds on, whether or not anyone chose it.

faqs.a: Till is sediment dropped directly by glacial ice, without being sorted by water. It is a jumble of clay, silt, sand, gravel and boulders mixed together with no layering, and it blankets much of Canada and the northern US.

An ice sheet scrapes and grinds the ground it crosses and carries the debris in and beneath the ice. Some is plastered down under the moving ice as dense lodgement till; the rest drops loosely as the ice melts, as ablation till.

faqs.q: How can you tell till from outwash?
faqs.a: Till is unsorted: boulders sit in clay beside pebbles, with no layers. Outwash was sorted by meltwater: clean, rounded sand and gravel in distinct beds. A gravel pit or road cut usually makes the difference obvious.

Across nearly all the land the ice sheets covered: most of Canada, New England, the Great Lakes states and the northern plains. Not everywhere, though — parts of the Yukon and Alaska stayed ice-free, and so did the Driftless Area of Wisconsin, Iowa and Minnesota.

name: Glacial outwash
tagline: Sand and gravel sorted by meltwater rivers pouring off a retreating ice sheet — droughty ground, and excellent aquifers.
forms: Rivers of meltwater braid away from the ice front, carrying colossal sediment loads. They drop gravel first, then sand, further out, building flat terraces and long ridges where a stream ran in an ice tunnel.
type: Surficial deposit — sand and gravel laid down by glacial meltwater
madeOf: Mostly quartz and feldspar sand, with pebbles of whatever rock the ice carried.
grain: Sorted and layered sand and gravel with moderately well-rounded grains; cross-bedding shows which way the meltwater ran.
colour: Tan, grey or brown sand, with gravel in the mixed colours of whatever rock the ice carried.
luster: Not a rock, so no luster of its own; quartz sand grains glint.
streak: Not a streak material.
hardness: Not rock: loose sand and gravel you can dig with a shovel.
density: Varies with grain size and packing; there is no single figure for loose sediment.
porosity: High: sand is typically 20–35% open space, gravel 30–40%, and water moves through both freely.
acid: In places — only where calcite is part of the mix.
formsFrom: Debris released from melting glacial ice, washed out and sorted by meltwater streams in front of the glacier.
becomes: Sandstone and conglomerate if it is ever buried and cemented; for now, dry, sandy soil.
howLong: Laid down as the last ice sheets melted back: Cape Cod's outwash plains and moraines are about 16,000 to 20,000 years old.
world: In front of every former ice sheet and glacier, and forming today wherever glaciers are melting.
what: The sorted counterpart to till. Meltwater had energy and sorting power that ice did not, so it separated the material by size and laid it in beds across broad flat plains.
identify: Well-sorted, rounded, layered sand and gravel, on flat terraces or in long sinuous ridges. Pits dug into it stand in clean horizontal beds.
wears: Barely — it is loose already, and water moves through it freely.
above: Droughty, sharply drained, low-fertility ground that warms early in spring. Excellent aquifers beneath, and the flat terraces make the easiest building land in glaciated country.
where: The outwash plains of Cape Cod and Long Island, the sand plains of Ontario and Quebec, and the outwash aprons along every northern valley.
lives: Pitch pine, jack pine and oak barrens, blueberry, and the sandy openings that ground-nesting birds and native bees need.
uses: The continent's sand and gravel supply, and a large share of its municipal well water.

faqs.a: Outwash is sand and gravel washed out of a melting glacier and laid down by meltwater streams in front of it. Unlike till, it has been sorted by water, so it comes in clean, rounded, layered beds.

Meltwater pours off the front of a glacier in streams loaded with sediment. As they spread out and slow, they drop sand and gravel in broad, flat outwash plains. Streams that flowed in tunnels in or under the ice leave long, winding ridges called eskers.

faqs.q: Why is outwash a good aquifer?
faqs.a: Because it is clean, sorted sand and gravel — about 20–40% open space, with pores big enough for water to flow freely. In glaciated country, outwash is a primary source of well water and supplies much of the steady base flow of streams.

In front of every former ice margin. Much of Cape Cod and the south shore of Long Island are outwash plains, laid down beside the moraines that mark the edge of the last ice sheet, roughly 16,000 to 20,000 years ago.

name: Marine clay
ph: Soil pH depends on the clay's lime content
tagline: Clay and silt that settled on the floor of a sea left behind by the melting ice — farmland where it drains, and prone to landslides where it is disturbed.
forms: Where the weight of the ice sheet had pressed the land down, the sea followed the retreating ice onto the lowlands. Fine rock flour carried out by meltwater settled slowly onto the sea floor. In eastern Canada this was the Champlain Sea, which covered the St. Lawrence Lowland and reached up the Ottawa Valley about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago.
type: Surficial deposit — fine marine sediment (clay and silt)
madeOf: Clayey silt: the Geological Survey of Canada describes the Champlain Sea's Leda clay as composed of glacially ground, non-clay minerals. The map description of the Ottawa-area unit adds minor laminae of fine sand.
grain: Clay and silt: grains too small to see, smooth to the touch. Fine sand turns up as thin laminae in places.
colour: Grey tones dominate in the Ottawa-basin units described by the Geological Survey of Canada (light grey in some, dark grey in others), with reddish layers more common in the Ottawa valley than in the Gatineau valley (Paper 85-21). The map description of the Ottawa-area unit lists many more, from pink and red-brown to olive, blue-grey and black.
luster: Dull and earthy.
streak: Not a streak material.
hardness: Not rock. The map description of the Ottawa-area unit reads: stiff; plastic and slippery where damp, tough and intensely fractured where dry.
density: Varies with water content; there is no single figure for a loose sediment.
porosity: Holds a lot of water in a loose structure (Geological Survey of Canada), but the pores are so fine that water moves through it very slowly.
acid: Often a little: the map description of the Ottawa-area unit says it is generally calcareous, meaning it contains lime, which fizzes in acid.
formsFrom: Rock flour and other fine sediment carried by glacial meltwater into a sea and settled on its floor.
becomes: Shale or mudstone, if it were ever buried and compacted; for now, farm soil and the banks of river valleys.
howLong: The Champlain Sea lasted roughly 2,000 years, about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago (The Canadian Encyclopedia).
world: The St. Lawrence Lowland and the Ottawa Valley, the area the Champlain Sea covered: about 55,000 km² between Quebec City and Brockville and up the Ottawa River valley (The Canadian Encyclopedia).
what: Clay and silt that settled on the floor of the sea that flooded the lowlands as the ice melted. In the Ottawa and St. Lawrence valleys it is the Champlain Sea's Leda clay, which the Geological Survey of Canada describes as a clayey silt of glacially ground, non-clay minerals.
identify: Smooth, fine and sticky when wet, hard and cracked into blocks when dry. A moist pinch rolled between finger and thumb makes a ribbon. Shells of salt- or brackish-water molluscs turn up in places, which is how geologists know it was laid down in the sea.
wears: It is already fine sediment, so it does not weather like rock. Streams cut gullies in it, and the map description of the Ottawa-area unit calls it very susceptible to landslide activity. Disturbed sensitive clay can lose its strength and flow like a liquid (Geological Survey of Canada).
above: Heavy, fine-grained ground: stiff, plastic and slippery where damp and cracked into blocks where dry (map description). Properly drained, Champlain Sea clay makes the best farmland in Quebec (The Canadian Encyclopedia). Beside rivers and cuts it can slide.
where: The St. Lawrence Lowland and the Ottawa Valley, in the area the Champlain Sea covered: from Quebec City to Brockville and up the Ottawa River valley.
lives: Farm crops, where it is drained. The shells of salt- and brackish-water molluscs are common in the clay itself (map description).
uses: Farmland, where it is drained. It is also the ground engineers have to plan around, because disturbed sensitive clay can lose strength and flow.

faqs.a: Clay and silt that settled on the floor of a sea. In the Ottawa and St. Lawrence valleys it was laid down in the Champlain Sea, about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago, and is often called Leda clay.

The name for the Champlain Sea's clay. The Geological Survey of Canada describes it as a clayey silt composed of glacially ground, non-clay minerals, held in a loose structure that can hold a lot of water.

faqs.q: Why does marine clay cause landslides?
faqs.a: Some of it is sensitive: if disturbed, it can lose strength, collapse and behave like a liquid. The Canadian Encyclopedia lists landslides in Champlain Sea clays at the Saint-Maurice Valley (1663), Saint-Alban (1894) and Nicolet (1955), and the Geological Survey of Canada documents an earthflow in sensitive Champlain Sea sediments at Lemieux, in the South Nation River valley, in 1993.

faqs.q: Is marine clay good for farming?
faqs.a: Where it is properly drained, yes: The Canadian Encyclopedia calls the drained Champlain Sea clays the best agricultural land in Quebec. The map description of the Ottawa-area unit calls it stiff, and plastic and slippery where damp.
